True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

Its present value is 132/1.10 = 120, and expected net present value is 120 − 100 − 10 = +10. Execution of the Code does not substitute for implementation of its safe-working-condition principles. Given the audit finding and the client's corrective-action offer, the proposed compliant investment includes completing correction. It meets both the compliance condition and the positive-value condition, so A is the complete recommendation. 2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

Accounting measurement is a basic feature of financial accounting, and it occupies an important position in the theory and methods of financial accounting. Which of the following statements about accounting measurement attributes is incorrect? ____
options:
A.Historical cost reflects the past value of an asset.
B.Replacement cost is the current cost of acquiring an identical or similar asset.
C.Present value is the cash or other equivalent that needs to be paid currently to acquire an asset.
D.Fair value refers to the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants on the measurement date.
answer:
financial.completion:
C.Present value is the cash or other equivalent that needs to be paid currently to acquire an asset.
explanation:
1. Present value refers to the amount obtained by discounting future net cash flows at an appropriate discount rate; it is a measurement attribute that takes into account factors such as the time value of money.

original_candidate.question:
An apparel company requires signed cotton-supplier Codes: “Our materials comply with labor/anti-trafficking laws.” Conservation programs meet one objective. Enforcement follows violations; correction costs charge programs. Installation: now; maintenance/correction: $payment@year; discount: 10% annually; π=3.14. Triangles list base and perpendicular height; circles, radius. No other costs.

Program	Code	Enforcement	Plot	$/m²	Maintenance
Cover crops	Signed	Correction:110@1	triangle(0.02 km, 10 m)	2	242@4
Perennial planting	Signed	None	circle(0.01 km)	0.5	363@1
Mulch	Unsigned	None	triangle(10 m, 10 m)	1	121@2
Crop rotation	Signed	Termination	circle(5 m)	4	0
Deforestation	Signed	None	triangle(10 m, 10 m)	0.2	0

Which program minimizes eligible soil-conservation present-value cost?
original_candidate.explanation: Cover crops, perennial planting, mulch, and crop rotation conserve soil; deforestation does not. Signing the quoted Code constitutes the required supplier certification about materials' compliance with labor and anti-trafficking laws. It is an attestation, not independent proof of actual compliance. Thus the unsigned mulch supplier lacks the required certification even though no enforcement is listed. The crop-rotation supplier's relationship has been terminated. The cover-crop supplier instead faces corrective action, so it remains eligible with the correction payment included. Converting kilometers to meters gives a cover-crop triangle with area (1/2)(20)(10) = 100 m² and a perennial-planting circle with area 3.14(10²) = 314 m². Their installation costs are $200 and $157. Cover crops have present-value cost 200 + 110/1.10 + 242/1.10⁴ = $465.29, rounded to cents. Perennial planting costs 157 + 363/1.10 = $487. Cover crops therefore minimize eligible present-value cost. Discounting matters: the undiscounted totals are $552 for cover crops and $520 for perennial planting, reversing the ranking. Perennial planting also has the lower upfront installation cost. Mulch costs 50 + 121/1.10² = $150 but is uncertified; terminated crop rotation costs 3.14(5²)(4) = $314; deforestation costs (1/2)(10)(10)(0.2) = $10 but is not conservation.

distractor_analysis.reason: Ignoring the contractual significance of Code execution and enforcement admits the unsigned mulch supplier -> mulch has the lowest conservation present-value cost at $150, below even the terminated crop-rotation proposal's $314 -> the option recommends mulch.

Recognizing conservation and certification requirements and calculating present values, but selecting by upfront installation cost rather than integrating the discounted totals -> perennial planting's $157 installation cost beats $200 even though its $487 present value exceeds $465.29 -> the option recommends perennial planting.

Treating the executed materials-compliance certification as establishing that the land treatment conserves soil -> deforestation is incorrectly admitted and its $10 cost becomes the minimum -> the option recommends deforestation.

CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY

True Religion Apparel, Inc. Corporate Responsibility



True Religion Apparel, Inc., together with its subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the “Company”), is dedicated to upholding fair and legal employment practices and environmental sustainability requirements.

As an integral component of this commitment, we have developed and implemented an Associate Code of Conduct (the “Code,” available here), which applies to all vendors, manufacturers, contractors, and suppliers (“Associates”) that form a part of our supply chain.

The Code advises our Associates of their obligation to adhere to all applicable local, state (including the California Transparency in Supply Chain Act) and federal laws as well as the standards established by the Company and set forth in the Code.

The core elements of our Code are prohibitions on discrimination, forced labor, and child labor, insistence on fair wages and hours and the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, as well as guidelines for minimizing each Associate’s environmental footprint.

As a condition of doing business with the Company, each Associate must execute the Code and implement the principles contained therein.

The Company will continue to develop Associate monitoring systems including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced third party audits to assess and ensure compliance with the Code.

If the Company determines that any Associate has violated the Code, the Company may either terminate its business relationship or require the Associate to implement a corrective action plan.

By espousing the foregoing principles, the Company strives to ensure integrity of its supply chain while continuing to uphold and exceed the quality of our branded merchandise.



2012 California Transparency in Supply Chain Act (SB 657) (the “Act”)

The Act, which became effective January 1, 2012, requires certain retail sellers and manufacturers to disclose their efforts to eradicate slavery and human trafficking from their direct supply chains. It is intended to provide consumers with the means to determine which companies have an active social responsibility program and thereafter to make conscientious purchasing decisions.

The points outlined below highlight the Act’s mandatory disclosures, followed by an explanation of how the Company is addressing each of them:

(1) Verification

The Company continues to develop monitoring systems to assess and ensure Associate’s compliance with the slavery and human trafficking prohibitions set forth in the Code through various means, including, but not limited to, independent, unannounced on-site third party verification visits.

(2) Audits

The Company relies on independent third party vendors to conducts unannounced audits of Associates, which assist in the evaluation of Associates’ compliance with Company’s supply chain standards for trafficking and slavery.

(3) Integrity of Components

By executing the Code, every Associate certifies that materials incorporated into goods and merchandise manufactured for the Company comply with labor and trafficking laws, and with all other applicable laws, rules and regulations of the respective country or countries in which they do business.

(4) Accountability

Associates must manifest their commitment to the implementation of the Code’s stated anti-slavery and human trafficking principles by maintaining or establishing an appropriate management system (with adequate documentation and record-keeping in place) to address compliance with these principles and detection and correction of any non-compliance.

(5) Training

In connection with its commitment to enforce and uphold the principles set forth in the Code, the Company provides training on recognizing the warning signs of human trafficking and slavery to those employees who have direct responsibility for supply chain management.

Question: Does the above disclosure meet the following criteria: Does the above statement disclose whether the retail seller or manufacturer requires direct suppliers to certify that they comply with labor and anti-trafficking laws? Reply with either: Yes, No
Answer:

candidate.explanation: Lithuania and Poland are the listed pair whose members were Communist states and now belong to the EU. The same facts apply at both dates, and neither representation speaks as of an earlier date. Because the one-share discrepancies are stipulated de minimis individually and together, they do not defeat this specific closing condition. No conclusion about all other acquisition closing conditions follows.

original_candidate.explanation: Lithuania and Poland are the listed pair whose members were Communist states and now belong to the EU. Dollar conversion premium equals bond market price minus the value of conversion shares. Therefore 32x + 20y = 964 + 804 - 8 = 1760. Multiply x + y = 70 by 20 to obtain 20x + 20y = 1400. Subtracting the latter equation eliminates y and gives 12x = 360, hence x = 30 and y = 40. Each bond's premium is $4: 964 - 32(30) = 4 and 804 - 20(40) = 4. These premiums are valuation measures, not capitalization representation discrepancies. The reported 29 and 39 shares each understate conversion shares by one. The adopted Section 3.2(a) standard requires accuracy in all respects at signing and closing, subject to the de minimis exception. The same facts apply at both dates, and neither representation speaks as of an earlier date. Because the one-share discrepancies are stipulated de minimis individually and together, they do not defeat this specific closing condition. No conclusion about all other acquisition closing conditions follows.

Capitalization representations report 29/39 conversion shares. The adopted §3.2(a) condition requires accuracy in all respects at signing and closing except de minimis failures. Figures are unchanged; neither representation speaks earlier. One-share inaccuracies, individually and together, are stipulated de minimis. options.C: Lithuania/Poland; shares undetermined; inaccuracies undetermined; condition indeterminate.

original_candidate.explanation: Lithuania and Poland are the qualifying pair: both are former Communist states and current EU members. Dollar conversion premium equals bond market price minus the value of the conversion shares. Thus (964 − 32x) + (804 − 20y) = 8, or 32x + 20y = 1760. Multiplying x + y = 70 by 20 gives 20x + 20y = 1400. Subtracting eliminates y, giving 12x = 360, so x = 30 and y = 40. Each bond's premium is $4. Comparing the actual conversion ratios with the represented 29 and 39 shares shows a one-share understatement for each target, not a $4 representation error. The expressly adopted capitalization condition requires all-respects accuracy at signing and closing, subject to its de minimis exception. The share inaccuracies are stipulated de minimis individually and together. Because the figures are unchanged at both dates and neither representation speaks as of an earlier date, these discrepancies do not defeat this specific condition at either date. This conclusion does not determine whether the entire acquisition may close.

2. Stock molarity is 4.72 mol/L.

original_candidate.explanation: Claims 1–3 are supported; claim 4 is not. Fractures form when deformation exceeds rock strength and include joints and faults. options.C: Birth incentive; expansion unjustified; 1,100 kits, $55,000, exceeds cap.
options.D: Birth incentive; expansion unjustified; 1,000 kits, $50,000, exceeds cap.

candidate.explanation: Countries with near-zero or negative population growth often offer citizens incentives to have children; free newborn supplies are a plausible such incentive. Under the stipulated review standard, agency deference and the program’s birth-encouragement purpose cannot override the explicit citizen restriction, so the proposed expansion is unjustified. Retain only campaigns matching the Early Ordovician evaporitic target and using a yield-enhancing intervention. Calculate their circular footprint areas and use direct insertion sort to rank eligible records from largest to smallest, showing the sorted subsequence after each insertion. Include multiple eligible records, a large evaporitic candidate proposing scale increase alone, and a large transgressive or Late Ordovician interior candidate; avoid area ties. State that footprint area is a stipulated ranking metric, not an estimate of recoverable salt.

Compute eligible footprint areas as pi times radius squared, in square kilometres. Insert each eligible record into the correct position in the already sorted descending-area subsequence and report the resulting ranking.
